secondaryCondition: Peritoneal adhesions (post-surgical adhesive disease with recurrent or intermittent small-bowel obstruction) following cholecystectomy performed for service-connected cholelithiasis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7301 (peritoneum, adhesions of, due to surgery, trauma, disease, or infection): 80 percent for persistent partial bowel obstruction that is inoperable and refractory to treatment or requires total parenteral nutrition; 50 percent for symptomatic adhesions persisting or recurring after surgery with documented dietary modification and clinical evidence of recurrent obstruction requiring hospitalization at least once a year plus at least one of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, colic, constipation, or diarrhea; 30 percent for that same symptomatic pattern without the hospitalization requirement; 10 percent for symptomatic adhesions with at least one of those symptoms; 0 percent for a history of adhesions that is currently asymptomatic. DC 7301 is the code the schedule actually provides for this disability; the CRG catalog identity 'peritoneal-adhesions' currently carries only a framework citation (38 CFR 4.114) and no diagnosis-specific code, so the code asserted here is a schedule fact and not a catalog assignment. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected cholelithiasis requiring cholecystectomy, performed as an open procedure (the operative report establishing the open approach is the controlling document, not the veteran's recollection of the incision)
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) rated as DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic with no documented attack. DC 7318 covers complications of cholecystectomy (strictures, biliary leaks) and is a separate code from the cholelithiasis evaluation. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Surgical peritoneal-injury sequence. Opening the peritoneal cavity causes mesothelial injury, local ischemia at the operative site and an inflammatory exudate in which fibrinogen is converted to fibrin; the peritoneum's fibrinolytic capacity is simultaneously suppressed, so the fibrinous bridges that form in the first postoperative days are not lysed but are organized by fibroblast in-growth and angiogenesis into permanent collagenous adhesions that tether bowel to the abdominal wall, the liver bed or adjacent viscera. Those bands exert traction, kink the bowel and distort the mesentery, producing intermittent partial obstruction with colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension and constipation, and they can progress to complete small-bowel obstruction or internal herniation requiring emergency surgery; each adhesiolysis creates fresh peritoneal injury and fresh adhesions, so the process is self-reinforcing rather than self-limited. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory. The service-connected cholelithiasis is the legal and medical predicate for the operation, and a disability that is proximately due to or the result of treatment required by a service-connected disease is itself service connected; under § 3.310(a) once service connection is established the adhesion condition is treated as part of the original condition, but it is still rated separately under its own code, DC 7301, because the schedule provides a specific evaluation for peritoneal adhesions and rates them on obstruction frequency, hospitalization and dietary modification rather than on the biliary criteria. This is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory. Section 3.310(b) would govern only where the record shows pre-existing peritoneal adhesions from an earlier abdominal operation, endometriosis, intra-abdominal infection or peritonitis and the claim is that the later cholecystectomy measurably worsened a baseline adhesive burden; in that posture the new-surgery increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing adhesions and VA will not concede aggravation unless the baseline level of severity is established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the adhesions are at least as likely as not caused by the open cholecystectomy performed for the service-connected cholelithiasis therefore require: (1) documentation of the service-connected cholelithiasis; (2) an operative note establishing that an open cholecystectomy was performed and describing the peritoneal field; (3) an interval in which obstruction symptoms first appear after the operation rather than before it; and (4) objective findings of adhesive obstruction or tethering, that is, imaging showing a transition point, adhesions seen at reoperation, or operative findings of bands, rather than pain alone. Quantitative anchors for the strength of the causal bridge are procedure-specific. Barmparas and colleagues (PMID 20352368) pooled 446,331 abdominal operations and found an overall adhesive small-bowel-obstruction incidence of 4.6 percent, with an incidence of 7.1 percent after open cholecystectomy versus 0.2 percent after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Udelsman and colleagues (PMID 30499802) analyzed 1,612,629 Californian patients with a median follow-up of 6.3 years and found a 5-year adhesive small-bowel-obstruction incidence after cholecystectomy of 2.2 percent for open versus 0.65 percent for laparoscopic procedures, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.89 (P less than 0.001) for the open approach and the greatest risk concentrated in the first two postoperative years. Lorentzen and colleagues (PMID 29030779) reviewed 478 patients operated for adhesive small-bowel obstruction, found an overall recurrence rate of 12.1 percent over a median of 2.2 years, and showed that recurrence risk persisted for years after the index operation, with multiple or matted adhesions independently increasing risk. Three candid limitations must be carried on the face of any opinion. First, the strength of the theory is approach-dependent: laparoscopic cholecystectomy carries a substantially lower adhesion-related risk than open surgery, so a laparoscopic operation weakens but does not automatically defeat the claim and the operative report is decisive; where the record shows a laparoscopic approach, the examiner must explain what intraoperative conversion, spillage, retained gallstones or separate peritoneal closure supports the theory instead. Second, adhesions are an extremely common incidental finding in anyone who has undergone abdominal surgery, so the nexus opinion must link the specific symptom pattern to documented adhesive obstruction rather than to coexisting conditions. Third, competing causes must be excluded or weighed on the record, including hernia (including port-site and incisional hernia), malignancy, Crohn's disease, gallstone ileus, bezoar, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic constipation, gastroparesis, chronic cholecystitis and post-cholecystectomy syndrome, endometriosis, prior surgery in any quadrant, and peritonitis or abscess from the index biliary episode. No single-study probability is asserted as a disability probability here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and constipation may not be compensated simultaneously under the biliary code and again under the adhesion code, and where more than one rating is warranted within the digestive system the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture.

medicalEvidence.title: The incidence and risk factors of post-laparotomy adhesive small bowel obstruction.
medicalEvidence.authors: Barmparas G; Branco BC; Schnüriger B; Lam L; Inaba K; Demetriades D
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review pooling 446,331 abdominal operations found an overall adhesive small-bowel-obstruction incidence of 4.6 percent and, decisively for this mapping, a cholecystectomy-specific incidence of 7.1 percent after open cholecystectomy versus 0.2 percent after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with separate peritoneal closure and retention of gallstones during cholecystectomy identified as further risk factors. This is the study that makes the documented operative approach the controlling fact in the claim.

medicalEvidence.title: Population Level Analysis of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction: Sustained Advantage of a Laparoscopic Approach.
medicalEvidence.authors: Udelsman BV; Chang DC; Parina R; Talamini MA; Lillemoe KD; Witkowski ER
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-level analysis of 1,612,629 patients with median 6.3-year follow-up found a 5-year adhesive small-bowel-obstruction incidence after cholecystectomy of 2.2 percent for open versus 0.65 percent for laparoscopic procedures, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.89 (P less than 0.001) for the open approach and the period of greatest risk within the first two postoperative years. Supplies both the surgical-trauma gradient and the postoperative time window an examiner should expect.

medicalEvidence.title: Recurrence After Operative Treatment of Adhesive Small-Bowel Obstruction.
medicalEvidence.authors: Lorentzen L; Øines MN; Oma E; Jensen KK; Jorgensen LN
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of 478 patients undergoing emergency surgery for adhesive small-bowel obstruction found an overall recurrence rate of 12.1 percent over a median 2.2-year follow-up, with risk persisting several years after the index operation and multiple or matted adhesions independently increasing recurrence. Establishes the chronicity that separates a compensable adhesion condition from a single transient postoperative event.

secondaryCondition: Osteomalacia (defective bone mineralization within the chronic-kidney-disease mineral and bone disorder spectrum, with bone pain, proximal myopathy and fragility fracture risk) in a veteran with service-connected chronic kidney disease
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5014 (osteomalacia, residuals of) — rated under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024, which evaluates the listed bone diseases on limitation of motion of the affected parts; because osteomalacia frequently presents with diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy and fracture rather than with joint limitation of motion, a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required, and residual fractures are separately rated under the fracture codes. The CRG catalog identity 'osteomalacia' carries only a framework citation (38 CFR 4.71a) and no diagnosis-specific code, so DC 5014 is asserted here as the code the schedule actually provides rather than as a catalog assignment. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic kidney disease (chronic renal failure) with a documented reduction in glomerular filtration rate and laboratory evidence of disordered mineral metabolism (for example phosphate retention, elevated parathyroid hormone or fibroblast growth factor 23, or reduced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis) and DC 7502 (nephritis, chronic), each rated as renal dysfunction under the criteria of § 4.115a; DC 7537 (interstitial nephritis, including disorders of calcium metabolism) is the alternative code where that is the documented renal pathology. The schedule supplies no free-standing chronic-kidney-disease code, so the renal dysfunction evaluation under § 4.115a supplies the rating level. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Chronic-kidney-disease mineral and bone disorder sequence. Progressive loss of functional nephron mass reduces renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, calcitriol, so intestinal calcium absorption falls and the skeleton is progressively deprived of the mineral substrate it requires for normal osteoid mineralization; simultaneously, declining glomerular filtration retains phosphate, and the resulting hyperphosphatemia together with rising fibroblast growth factor 23 further suppresses calcitriol synthesis. The fall in ionized calcium and calcitriol, in combination with phosphate retention, drives secondary hyperparathyroidism, and parathyroid hormone excess in turn increases bone turnover, accelerates osteoclastic resorption and worsens the mineralization defect. The histological lesion is an accumulation of unmineralized osteoid with increased osteoid volume and thickness and a prolonged mineralization lag time: that is osteomalacia, one component of the mixed uremic osteodystrophy that defines chronic-kidney-disease mineral and bone disorder. Uremic toxin accumulation, metabolic acidosis and, historically, aluminium exposure from phosphate binders and dialysate contribute to the same mineralization failure. Clinically the untreated lesion produces diffuse deep bone pain, proximal muscle weakness with a waddling gait, and low-trauma fractures. Modest and colleagues (PMID 36173905) state expressly that causative factors of osteomalacia include renal insufficiency, and that renal osteodystrophy is a specific form of metabolic bone disease defined by the presence of osteomalacia and associated hyperparathyroidism secondary to malfunction or absence of renal parenchyma reducing conversion of vitamin D to its active form. Hou and colleagues (PMID 30298663) describe chronic-kidney-disease mineral and bone disorder as abnormal metabolism of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D together with abnormalities of bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth or strength and soft-tissue calcification, and explain that disordered bone turnover driven by uremic toxin or secondary hyperparathyroidism disturbs bone mineralization and makes it difficult for calcium and inorganic phosphate to enter bone. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the service-connected renal disease is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated skeletal condition with its own diagnostic code at DC 5014 rather than being folded into the renal dysfunction evaluation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; but § 3.310(b) would become the governing framework where the record shows pre-existing osteomalacia from a non-service-connected cause, such as dietary vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption after bariatric or bowel surgery, coeliac disease, anticonvulsant therapy or a hypophosphatemic disorder, and the claim is that the renal disease measurably worsened that baseline. In that posture the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the osteomalacia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected chronic kidney disease therefore require: (1) an established diagnosis of chronic kidney disease with a documented glomerular filtration rate and duration; (2) laboratory evidence of disordered mineral metabolism, which is the mechanistic link and not a mere association; (3) skeletal findings reasonably attributable to defective mineralization rather than to osteoporosis alone, such as low-trauma fracture, bone pain with elevated alkaline phosphatase, or biopsy or imaging evidence; and (4) exclusion of the competing causes listed above. Two candid limitations must be carried on the face of any opinion. First, non-invasive tests do not reliably discriminate between osteoporosis and the several forms of renal osteodystrophy: Pazianas and Miller (PMID 33774081) explain that neither laboratory nor non-invasive diagnostic investigations can make that discrimination and that transiliac crest bone biopsy, which is of limited availability, is what permits the diagnosis of osteoporosis by exclusion of other kidney-associated bone diseases. A claim therefore cannot be sustained on a bone density reading alone, and the examiner should say so. Second, chronic kidney disease is itself rated on renal dysfunction criteria under § 4.115a, so rating discipline under § 4.14 requires that the same functional impairment not be compensated twice, and where more than one skeletal evaluation is warranted the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include senile and postmenopausal osteoporosis with no mineralization defect, primary hyperparathyroidism, hypophosphatemic disorders including tumour-induced and X-linked hypophosphatemic osteomalacia, vitamin D deficiency from diet, sun avoidance or malabsorption, coeliac and inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, chronic liver disease and anticonvulsant or phosphate-binder therapy, and, in the dialysis population, dialysis-related amyloidosis and aluminium or iron overload. No single-study probability is asserted as a disability probability here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteomalacia and Renal Osteodystrophy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Modest JM; Sheth H; Gohh R; Aaron RK
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review defining osteomalacia as the undermineralization of newly formed bone due to a lack of available calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D, listing renal insufficiency among its causative factors, and defining renal osteodystrophy as the specific metabolic bone disease characterised by osteomalacia with associated hyperparathyroidism secondary to malfunction or absence of renal parenchyma that reduces conversion of vitamin D to its active form. The most direct statement in this row's evidence that chronic kidney disease produces osteomalacia.

medicalEvidence.title: Mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease.
medicalEvidence.authors: Hou YC; Lu CL; Lu KC
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of chronic-kidney-disease mineral and bone disorder showing that as glomerular filtration loss progresses the disturbed mineral metabolism worsens bone microstructure and remodelling, that the disorder is characterised by abnormal metabolism of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D together with abnormalities of bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth or strength, and that disregulated bone turnover from uremic toxin or secondary hyperparathyroidism disturbs bone mineralization so that calcium and inorganic phosphate cannot enter bone.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteoporosis and Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD): Back to Basics.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing that, on bone histology, osteoporosis is only part of a spectrum of skeletal complications that includes osteomalacia and the various forms of renal osteodystrophy, and — as a limitation the examiner must carry — that neither laboratory nor non-invasive diagnostic investigations can discriminate osteoporosis from the several forms of renal osteodystrophy, with transiliac crest bone biopsy (limited availability) required to make the diagnosis by exclusion of other kidney-associated bone diseases.

secondaryCondition: Raynaud's syndrome (secondary Raynaud's phenomenon with digital vasospasm, and its digital ulcer and auto-amputation sequelae) in a veteran with service-connected systemic sclerosis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7117 (Raynaud's syndrome (also known as secondary Raynaud's phenomenon or secondary Raynaud's)): 100 percent with two or more digital ulcers plus auto-amputation of one or more digits and a history of characteristic attacks; 60 percent with two or more digital ulcers and a history of characteristic attacks; 40 percent for characteristic attacks occurring at least daily; 20 percent for attacks four to six times a week; 10 percent for attacks one to three times a week. The schedule note states that these evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole regardless of the number of extremities involved. DC 7124 governs primary Raynaud's disease only and must not be used for a secondary form. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), with documented cutaneous or visceral involvement meeting accepted classification criteria
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7821 (cutaneous manifestations of collagen-vascular diseases not listed elsewhere (including scleroderma, calcinosis cutis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and dermatomyositis)), evaluated under the General Rating Formula for the Skin; visceral involvement is separately rated in the affected body system, for example oesophageal disease under § 4.114 or renal involvement under § 4.115. One catalog discrepancy is flagged for review: the CRG identity 'scleroderma' currently carries a framework citation of 38 CFR 4.117 (hemic and lymphatic systems), which does not contain DC 7821; the skin-schedule citation asserted here follows the authored mapping in the wave-12 packet. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Microvascular and fibrotic vascular sequence. In systemic sclerosis the earliest event is endothelial injury, followed by intimal proliferation and a progressive obliterative vasculopathy that structurally narrows the digital arteries and arterioles. Superimposed on that fixed narrowing is a functional shift toward vasoconstriction: platelet activation, increased endothelin-1 signalling, reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin availability and altered alpha-2c-adrenoreceptor and Rho-kinase signalling raise vascular tone and blunt endothelium-dependent vasodilation. The result is an exaggerated, initially reversible digital vasospasm in response to cold or emotional stress — Raynaud's phenomenon — which in systemic sclerosis is not a benign primary disorder but a marker and a driver of progressive digital ischemia. When vasospasm and fixed structural narrowing coexist, persistent hypoperfusion produces digital pitting scars, ischemic ulcers and auto-amputation of fingertips, and the same vasculopathy underlies pulmonary arterial hypertension and renal crisis elsewhere in the disease. Hughes and colleagues (PMID 32099191) state that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation to occur, and that it is caused by impaired digital perfusion and requires careful assessment to avoid missing secondary causes. Sunderkötter and Riemekasten (PMID 16987831) describe Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis, characterised by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress, and emphasise that structural alteration of the involved vessels, not merely a vasomotor imbalance, is fundamental to secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and explains why secondary Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis, unlike the primary form, leads to ischemic and reperfusion injury. Maciejewska and colleagues (PMID 35566614) state that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, and that identification of the secondary form changes the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory. The service-connected systemic sclerosis is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated vascular condition that has its own diagnostic code at DC 7117 with a severity staircase running from weekly attacks to digital ulcers with auto-amputation, so the Raynaud's syndrome is not folded into the skin evaluation at DC 7821 and receives its own evaluation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; § 3.310(b) would govern only where the record shows pre-existing primary Raynaud's disease, or cold-injury-related vasospasm, antedating the systemic sclerosis and the claim is that the sclerosis measurably worsened that baseline, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, DC 7124 rather than DC 7117 characterises the pre-existing condition, and the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the primary disorder. A chronology point cuts both ways and must be handled explicitly in the opinion. Because Raynaud's phenomenon is frequently the earliest manifestation of systemic sclerosis and can precede the diagnosis by years, an onset date for the vasospastic attacks that lies before the recorded diagnosis of systemic sclerosis does not defeat causation when the systemic sclerosis is later established by classification criteria; the correct reading is that the Raynaud's phenomenon was the first clinical expression of the same disease process. Equally, however, a veteran with vasospastic attacks and no features of systemic sclerosis has the primary disorder at DC 7124, which is a different entity and does not produce the ischemic ulceration spectrum. Evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the Raynaud's syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected systemic sclerosis therefore requires: (1) documentation of systemic sclerosis by accepted classification features, such as sclerodactyly, proximal skin thickening, specific autoantibodies (for example anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I or anti-RNA polymerase III), nailfold capillary abnormalities or internal-organ involvement; (2) a clinical description of characteristic attacks as the schedule's note defines them, namely sequential digital colour change lasting minutes to hours, precipitated by cold or emotional stress; (3) a temporal relationship in which the attacks begin with or after disease onset, or, where they precede the diagnosis, evidence that they were the presenting feature of the subsequently confirmed sclerosis; and (4) for the 60 and 100 percent tiers, documentation of digital ulcers or auto-amputation by examination, imaging or photography. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include primary Raynaud's disease (the schedule's separate DC 7124 entity), cold-injury residuals, cigarette smoking and other vasoconstrictor exposure, beta-blocker, ergotamine or stimulant medication, hypothyroidism, carpal tunnel and thoracic outlet syndromes, vibration-tool exposure, cryoglobulinemia and other connective-tissue diseases such as mixed connective-tissue disease or systemic lupus erythematosus, which are distinct service-connected or non-service-connected identities and must not be merged with systemic sclerosis. Rating discipline under § 4.14: because DC 7117 evaluates Raynaud's syndrome as a whole across all extremities, the same digital attacks, ulcers or amputations may not be compensated a second time under the scleroderma skin evaluation or under the cold-injury code, and separate amputation ratings follow only the schedule's own amputation provisions. No single-study probability is asserted as a disability probability here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Raynaud phenomenon and digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Hughes M; Allanore Y; Chung L; Pauling JD; Denton CP; Matucci-Cerinic M
medicalEvidence.summary: Review stating that Raynaud phenomenon is a symptom complex caused by impaired digital perfusion that occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation to occur, that careful assessment is required to avoid missing secondary causes such as systemic sclerosis, and that digital ulcers are a painful and disabling visible manifestation of digital vascular injury in the same disease. Primary evidence that the vasospastic disorder is a manifestation of the sclerosis rather than an unrelated condition.

medicalEvidence.title: Pathophysiology and clinical consequences of Raynaud's phenomenon related to systemic sclerosis.
medicalEvidence.summary: Article presenting Raynaud's phenomenon as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis in systemic sclerosis, characterised by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress, and explaining that structural alteration of the involved vessels, in addition to vasoconstrictive and vasodilatory imbalance, is fundamental to secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and the reason it leads to ischemic and reperfusion injury. Supplies the mechanistic account asserted in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Raynaud's Phenomenon with Focus on Systemic Sclerosis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Maciejewska M; Sikora M; Maciejewski C; Alda-Malicka R; Czuwara J; Rudnicka L
medicalEvidence.summary: Review reporting that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, and that treatment differs by underlying cause, with capillaroscopy fundamental to differentiating primary from secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and useful in the very early stages of systemic sclerosis. Supplies the classification evidence distinguishing secondary from primary Raynaud's phenomenon.

secondaryCondition: Aortic aneurysm (ascending, thoracic or abdominal) in a veteran with chronic service-connected hypertension, asserted as a § 3.310(a) formation theory; the § 3.310(b) aggravation theory is analysed and rejected below on the strength of the expansion evidence
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7110 (aortic aneurysm: ascending, thoracic or abdominal), evaluated at 100 percent only when the aneurysm is 5 centimeters or larger, symptomatic, or has required surgery, and otherwise at 0 percent. That tier structure is decisive for how this row must be pleaded: because a small, asymptomatic aneurysm has no compensable evaluation, a veteran whose causation theory succeeds may still receive no monetary award, and a veteran whose aggravation theory fails loses the increment entirely. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension), with chronic blood-pressure elevation documented by readings taken on at least three different days and, where the record permits, a documented duration and treatment history
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease; hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension), confirmed by readings taken on at least three different days, with the evaluation determined by the predominant diastolic and systolic levels documented in the record rather than by the number of readings alone. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Hemodynamic and matrix-degradation sequence. The abdominal aorta is the segment most exposed to repetitive pulsatile wall stress and is the segment where aneurysm disease overwhelmingly develops; chronic elevation of blood pressure increases that transmural stress and, over years, drives a degenerative remodelling cascade in the aortic media. Elastin fibres fragment under cyclic loading, collagen is progressively degraded, matrix metalloproteinases released by resident and infiltrating cells digest the extracellular matrix, vascular smooth muscle cells shift phenotype from a contractile to a synthetic and pro-inflammatory state and undergo apoptosis, and a chronic macrophage and lymphocyte infiltrate with neovascularisation weakens the wall further. Because the wall's load-bearing capacity falls while the luminal pressure it must contain remains elevated, the aorta dilates in an attempt to normalise wall tension, and that dilation is the aneurysm. Qian and colleagues (PMID 35207478) describe abdominal aortic aneurysm as a lethal degenerative vascular disease characterised by aortic wall inflammation, elastin breakdown, oxidative stress, smooth-muscle-cell phenotypic switching and dysfunction and extracellular matrix degradation, and review the risk factors and pathophysiology that make the wall a pressure-loaded, inflammation-degraded structure. Kobeissi and colleagues (PMID 30903463), a meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies with 28,162 cases among 5,440,588 participants, found a summary relative risk of abdominal aortic aneurysm of 1.66 (95 percent confidence interval 1.49 to 1.85) in hypertensive compared with non-hypertensive patients, a 14 percent increase in relative risk (95 percent confidence interval 6 to 23 percent) per 20 millimetres of mercury of systolic blood pressure and a 28 percent increase (95 percent confidence interval 12 to 46 percent) per 10 millimetres of mercury of diastolic blood pressure, with a non-linear diastolic dose-response that steepens from 80 millimetres of mercury upward. Altobelli and colleagues (PMID 30544688) found that aneurysm prevalence is higher in smokers and in males and that diabetes, while a risk factor for many cardiovascular diseases, is not a risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this row is deliberately pleaded as a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory, that is, that the service-connected hypertension caused the aneurysm to form, and not as a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory that service-connected hypertension accelerated the growth of a pre-existing non-service-connected aneurysm. The reason is evidentiary and is central to the integrity of this mapping. Section 3.310(b) makes compensable only the increase in severity of a non-service-connected disease that is proximately due to the service-connected disease and not due to the natural progress of the non-service-connected disease; VA will not concede aggravation unless the baseline level of severity is established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest medical evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the receipt of evidence establishing the current level of severity, and the rating activity then deducts both the baseline and any increase due to natural progression from the current level. The best available synthesis directly on the growth question is negative: Takagi and colleagues (PMID 27521823), a meta-analysis of 20 studies including 6,619 patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm, found that hypertension was not associated with aneurysm expansion rates (pooled standardised mean difference 0.03, 95 percent confidence interval minus 0.01 to 0.17, P equals 0.19), and no individual study showed a statistically significant association in either direction. That null result is not the end of the scientific question, because serial ultrasound measurement error is of the same order as annual growth, the cohorts were overwhelmingly composed of patients already receiving antihypertensive therapy so any pressure-dependent growth effect would be attenuated by treatment, and observational expansion cohorts are subject to selection and survival bias; but it does mean that an examiner cannot honestly state that the literature supports hypertension-driven acceleration of an existing aneurysm. The defensible theory is therefore formation, which the dose-response incidence data and the wall-stress mechanism support, and the aggravation theory should be pleaded, if at all, only with an explicit acknowledgement that the supporting evidence is weaker than the incidence evidence and that the baseline measurement required by § 3.310(b) must already exist in the record. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the aneurysm is at least as likely as not proximately due to the service-connected hypertension therefore require: (1) a documented history of chronic hypertension, ideally antedating the first imaging evidence of aneurysm; (2) imaging that measures the aneurysm and states its anatomical segment and maximum diameter, since the diameter drives both the DC 7110 evaluation and the rupture-risk discussion; (3) an apportionment analysis that confronts the dominant competing cause, cigarette smoking, together with age, male sex, family history of aneurysm, connective-tissue disease such as Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vasculitis including giant-cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis, prior aortic dissection or trauma, and bicuspid aortic valve disease with ascending-aortic involvement; and (4) a statement of what proportion, if any, of the aneurysm is attributable to the service-connected hypertension rather than to those competing causes, because a nexus opinion that does not apportion in a lifelong smoker is unlikely to withstand adjudication. Three further limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, because the 0 percent and 100 percent tiers of DC 7110 are separated by a 5-centimetre, symptomatic or operated threshold, the practical value of the mapping is limited to aneurysms at or above that threshold, those requiring repair, or those producing symptoms; a 3.4 centimetre incidental aneurysm established at causation still yields no compensable evaluation. Second, the presumption in § 3.310(c) for ischemic heart disease and other cardiovascular disease in a veteran with service-connected lower-extremity amputation at or above the knee does not apply to this row and cannot be borrowed to supply causation. Third, rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same hypertension-driven vascular impairment from being compensated twice, and where hypertension itself is rated under DC 7101 the aneurysm evaluation under DC 7110 is separate and additive only to the extent the schedule provides. No single-study probability is asserted as a disability probability here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Blood pressure, hypertension and the risk of abdominal aortic aneurysms: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.
medicalEvidence.authors: Kobeissi E; Hibino M; Pan H; Aune D
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies (28,162 cases among 5,440,588 participants) finding a summary relative risk of abdominal aortic aneurysm of 1.66 (95 percent confidence interval 1.49 to 1.85) in hypertensive versus non-hypertensive patients, a 14 percent increase in relative risk per 20 millimetres of mercury of systolic blood pressure and 28 percent per 10 millimetres of mercury of diastolic blood pressure, with a non-linear diastolic dose-response steepening from 80 millimetres of mercury. Supplies both the effect size and the pressure dose-response that an apportionment analysis needs.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk Factors for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm in Population-Based Studies: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
medicalEvidence.authors: Altobelli E; Rapacchietta L; Profeta VF; Fagnano R
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of population-based studies reporting aneurysm prevalence between 1.3 and 12.5 percent that found prevalence higher in smokers and in males and, importantly for apportionment, that diabetes is not a risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm despite being a risk factor for many other cardiovascular diseases. Frames the competing-cause hierarchy the nexus opinion must confront, with smoking dominant.

medicalEvidence.title: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Formation with a Focus on Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells.
medicalEvidence.authors: Qian G; Adeyanju O; Olajuyin A; Guo X
medicalEvidence.summary: Review describing abdominal aortic aneurysm as a lethal degenerative vascular disease involving aortic wall inflammation, elastin breakdown, oxidative stress, smooth-muscle-cell phenotypic switching and dysfunction and extracellular matrix degradation, with a diameter criterion of greater than 30 millimetres or more than 50 percent of normal and with lifestyle and genetic predisposition increasing risk. Supplies the mechanistic anchor — the load-bearing wall is degraded by inflammation and matrix destruction while remaining pressure-loaded — that converts an epidemiological association into a physiological explanation.

secondaryCondition: Tardive dyskinesia associated with metoclopramide (medication-induced persistent choreoathetoid movement disorder, orofacial in distribution and potentially extending to the limbs and trunk, with speech, swallowing or gait consequences)
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated tardive-dyskinesia diagnostic code is listed in 38 CFR § 4.124a. A clinically justified analogous code under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is required, selected on the affected muscle groups and on the severity of the involuntary movements and of any speech, swallowing, gait or respiratory involvement. DC 8103 (convulsive tic) and DC 8004 (paralysis agitans) are candidate comparators only and are not automatically applicable, and no diagnostic code is invented here. The CRG catalog identity 'tardive-dyskinesia' carries an empty ratingSchedule array, which is consistent with this finding and with the repository's rule against inventing codes for movement disorders. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with metoclopramide (prokinetic and antiemetic therapy), with the actual documented indication, dose and duration confirmed from the medication record because long-term use is regulatory-restricted
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7206 (gastroesophageal reflux disease), evaluated on the frequency, severity and duration of reflux symptoms and on dysphagia, oesophageal stricture or other complications where those are present. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological dopamine-blockade sequence. Metoclopramide is primarily a dopamine receptor antagonist, with 5-HT3 receptor antagonist and 5-HT4 receptor agonist activity, used as an antiemetic and gastroprokinetic; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and at therapeutic doses blocks nigrostriatal dopamine receptors as well as the peripheral and chemoreceptor-trigger-zone receptors that produce its intended gastrointestinal effect. Prolonged blockade of the nigrostriatal pathway is followed by adaptive changes in the basal ganglia: postsynaptic dopamine receptor supersensitivity and up-regulation, altered striatal GABAergic and cholinergic output and maladaptive synaptic plasticity, which together unmask delayed-onset, persistent, involuntary choreoathetoid movements. In metoclopramide-induced disease the earliest and most characteristic distribution is orofacial, involving the tongue, lips, jaw and perioral muscles, and the disorder is often first reported by the patient or family as lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, grimacing or chewing movements rather than as a complaint of involuntary movement; at higher exposure the limbs and trunk may be involved, and the movements may worsen in the days after the drug is stopped (withdrawal-emergent worsening) before any plateau, and they may persist indefinitely. Al-Saffar and colleagues (PMID 31050085) state that metoclopramide is primarily a dopamine receptor antagonist with 5-HT3 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist activity, that regulatory authorities issued restrictions and recommendations regarding long-term use at oral doses exceeding 10 milligrams three to four times daily because of the risk of tardive dyskinesia, that the risk is in the range of 0.1 percent per 1,000 patient-years, far below the 1 to 10 percent previously suggested in regulatory treatment guidelines, and that the high-risk groups are elderly females, diabetics, patients with liver or kidney failure and patients on concomitant antipsychotic therapy, in whom the threshold for neurological complications is reduced. Rao and Camilleri (PMID 19886950) record that the United States Food and Drug Administration issued a black-box warning in 2009 regarding long-term or high-dose use of metoclopramide because of the risk of developing tardive dyskinesia, describe tardive dyskinesia as possibly an idiosyncratic response with pharmacogenetic determinants affecting drug handling and dopamine receptor pharmacodynamics, and estimate the risk of tardive dyskinesia from metoclopramide at likely less than 1 percent. Merrill and colleagues (PMID 23714238) provide the population denominator that any attribution analysis needs: in a claims-based cohort, the incidence rate of tardive dyskinesia per 1,000 exposed persons was 4.6 for antipsychotic use only, 8.5 for metoclopramide use only and 15.0 for both, the general-population incidence of tardive dyskinesia was 4.3 per 100,000 person-years, incidence rose with age and was greater in females, and persons with diabetes or psychoses had almost three times the risk of tardive dyskinesia while those with schizophrenia had 31.2 times the risk. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the treatment of the service-connected disability is the causal instrument. The metoclopramide was prescribed for the service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease, and a disability that is proximately due to or the result of the treatment required by a service-connected condition is itself service connected. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows a pre-existing movement disorder from earlier dopamine-blocking therapy — an antipsychotic, prochlorperazine, promethazine or another antiemetic — that antedated the metoclopramide course, or pre-existing orofacial dyskinesia; in that posture § 3.310(b) applies, the baseline level of severity must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the receipt of evidence establishing the current severity, the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder is deducted, and the opinion must apportion the contribution of each dopamine-blocking exposure rather than attributing all of the movements to metoclopramide. A second framing point is decisive in practice: the medication must have been prescribed for the service-connected condition. Where metoclopramide was prescribed for an indication that is not service connected, for example acute nausea after a viral illness or gastroparesis unrelated to the reflux diagnosis, the same movement disorder is not secondary to the service-connected disease, and the record must be read carefully for the indication actually documented at the time of prescribing. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the tardive dyskinesia is at least as likely as not caused by metoclopramide prescribed for the service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease therefore require: (1) documentation of metoclopramide exposure with start and stop dates, dose and cumulative duration taken from pharmacy or prescription records rather than from the veteran's recollection; (2) documentation that the service-connected reflux disease was the indication for which the drug was prescribed; (3) examination findings of persistent involuntary choreoathetoid movements with a recorded Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) score and a description of the affected muscle groups; (4) where the drug has been discontinued, persistence of the movements for a defined interval after discontinuation rather than an acute reaction at the time of a single dose; and (5) exclusion of the competing causes below. Four candid limitations must be carried on the face of any opinion. First, the risk is low — roughly 0.1 per 1,000 patient-years in the pooled regulatory estimate and less than 1 percent in the review estimate — so the existence of a metoclopramide prescription does not by itself carry the nexus; the opinion must rest on the individual's documented exposure, findings and chronology, and the low base rate means competing causes deserve particular scrutiny. Second, the reaction is at least partly idiosyncratic and pharmacogenetically determined, so the absence of high-dose or long-duration use weakens but does not automatically defeat the claim, and an examiner should not treat a standard dose as exculpatory. Third, spontaneous dyskinesia exists in the general population without any dopamine-blocking exposure, and Merrill and colleagues documented it directly; that finding is a competing cause that must be addressed on the record rather than ignored, along with other dopamine-blocking agents prescribed for non-service-connected conditions (antipsychotics, prochlorperazine and promethazine for nausea, and other antiemetics), drug-induced parkinsonism, edentulous orofacial dyskinesia and ill-fitting dentures, Huntington's disease, hyperthyroid chorea, Sydenham chorea, Wilson's disease, tic disorders including Tourette syndrome, cerebrovascular disease and pre-existing orofacial dyskinesia. Fourth, the diagnostic-code gap is real: because § 4.124a contains no tardive-dyskinesia code, the condition may be evaluated only by analogy under §§ 4.20 and 4.27, which limits the rating certainty of the claim but does not defeat service connection. Rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same impairment from being compensated twice, and the involuntary movements may not be compensated both as residuals of the medication reaction and again as part of a separate neurological evaluation for the same movements. No single-study probability is asserted as a disability probability here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Gastroparesis, metoclopramide, and tardive dyskinesia: Risk revisited.
medicalEvidence.authors: Al-Saffar A; Lennernäs H; Hellström PM
medicalEvidence.summary: Review showing that metoclopramide is primarily a dopamine receptor antagonist with 5-HT3 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist activity, that regulators restricted long-term use at oral doses exceeding 10 milligrams three to four times daily because of tardive-dyskinesia risk, that the risk is approximately 0.1 percent per 1,000 patient-years, and that high-risk groups are elderly females, diabetics, patients with liver or kidney failure and patients on concomitant antipsychotics. Supplies both the mechanism and the calibrated risk figure that keep the opinion honest.

medicalEvidence.title: Review article: metoclopramide and tardive dyskinesia.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review recording the 2009 Food and Drug Administration black-box warning for long-term or high-dose metoclopramide because of tardive-dyskinesia risk, reviewing the drug's mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics, estimating the risk of tardive dyskinesia at likely less than 1 percent, and characterising the reaction as possibly idiosyncratic with pharmacogenetic determinants affecting drug handling and dopamine receptor pharmacodynamics. Documents the regulatory finding that makes long-term use a departure from the standard of care.

medicalEvidence.title: Tardive and spontaneous dyskinesia incidence in the general population.
medicalEvidence.authors: Merrill RM; Lyon JL; Matiaco PM
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective population cohort (2001-2010 claims data) reporting tardive dyskinesia incidence of 4.6 per 1,000 persons exposed to antipsychotics only, 8.5 per 1,000 exposed to metoclopramide only and 15.0 per 1,000 exposed to both, a general-population tardive dyskinesia incidence of 4.3 per 100,000 person-years, rising incidence with age and in females, an approximately three-fold risk with diabetes or psychoses, and — as a limitation the examiner must carry — the existence of spontaneous dyskinesia in the general population measured on the same records.
